title: Maximum Binary Tree II
statement:
A **maximum tree** is a binary tree in which every node holds a larger value than anything else in its subtree. One is made from a list of distinct numbers by a routine `build(list)`:

- An empty list gives an empty tree (`null`).
- Otherwise the biggest number in the list becomes the root. Its left subtree is `build` of the numbers before that biggest number, and its right subtree is `build` of the numbers after it.

You receive `root`, the tree that `build(a)` produced for some list `a` that you never see, and an integer `val`. Let `b` be `a` with `val` added as its last element; `val` is guaranteed not to appear in `a`, so `b` still has distinct numbers. Return the root of `build(b)`.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 100 nodes
val does not occur in the tree
notes:
## Intuition

The slow way is to undo the construction: an in-order walk of a maximum tree gives back the hidden list `a`, so you could append `val` and rebuild, which costs O(n²). But `val` sits at the **end** of `b`, so it never changes anything to its left. At the root there are only two cases. If `val` is bigger than the root, it is the maximum of `b`: it becomes the new root and everything before it (the whole old tree) is its left subtree. Otherwise the old root stays the maximum, its left part of the list is untouched, and `val` joins the list to its right, so the same question repeats on the right subtree.

## Approach

1. If `root` is `null`, the list on this side was empty, so the answer is a single node holding `val`.
2. If `val > root.val`, create `node` for `val`, hang the whole current tree under `node.left`, and return `node`.
3. Otherwise replace `root.right` with the result of inserting `val` into it, and return `root`.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [4,1,3,null,null,2]` came from `a = [1,4,2,3]`, and `val = 5`. At the root, `5 > 4`, so a new `node` with value 5 is created, the tree rooted at 4 becomes its left child, and the result is `[5,4,null,1,3,null,null,2]`, which is `build([1,4,2,3,5])`. For contrast, in Example 2 (`root = [5,2,4,null,1]`, `val = 3`) the walk goes right from 5 to 4, finds `3 < 4`, moves on to 4's empty right side and attaches 3 there.

## Complexity

- Time: O(h), where h is the length of the path down the right edge (at most n): each step moves one node to the right.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion.

## Pitfalls

- Never step into the left subtree: `val` is last in `b`, so it always lands to the right of every existing value. Inserting as in a search tree gives the wrong shape.
- When `val` beats a node, that node's whole subtree becomes the **left** child of the new node, because all of it comes before `val` in `b`.
- Return the new node when it beats the root; returning the old `root` loses the new top of the tree.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the subtree currently being updated |
| `val` | the value appended to the hidden list |
| `node` | the new node for `val` when it is larger than `root.val` |

narration.2: An empty subtree means the list on this side was empty, so val stands alone.
narration.3: Return a single node holding val.
narration.5: Is val bigger than the current root? Then it is the maximum of this part of b.
narration.6: Create the node for val, which becomes the new top of this subtree.
narration.7: Everything in the old subtree comes before val in b, so it all goes to the left.
narration.8: Hand back the new node as the root of this subtree.
narration.10: Otherwise the root stays, and val belongs somewhere in the right subtree.
narration.11: Return the unchanged root, now with the updated right side.
